newsitem.title: USA: GM, UAW talks continuing despite walkout.
newsitem.headline: GM, UAW talks continuing despite walkout.

text.p: United Auto Worker President Stephen Yokich said on Thursday that bargaining continues between the union and General Motors Corp despite a strike at GM plants in Canada, but added that he did not know if a U.S. settlement could be reached during the Canadian walkout.

Speaking to reporters at a meeting of the UAW's National Chrysler Council, Yokich said the UAW needs to make some decisions on its own strategy and talk with leaders of the Canadian Auto Workers before deciding on how to proceed in U.S. negotiations.
"We have to make some decisions ourselves," Yokich said. "We were hoping our brothers and sisters in Canada could have settled."
More than 15,000 members of the Canadian Auto Workers union struck GM's Canadian assembly plants late on Wednesday as a deadline for a new labor pact expired.
Yokich said he is supportive of the CAW walkout, over job security issues, and would discuss the situation with CAW President Buzz Hargrove later today.
Yokich declined to speculate about when the UAW might reach an agreement with GM, saying, "I don't have a magic wand, I don't have a crystal ball."
The UAW reached a tentative agreement with Chrysler Corp on Sunday, surpising most analysts who did not think the two sides were close to a deal.
Yokich said he has been directly inolved with the GM-UAW talks over the last several days and will continue to participate. He said he has held a number of discussions with GM Chairman Jack Smith.

Yokich said he has not held any discussions with Harry Pearce, vice chairman of GM. Pearce has in the past taken a highly visible role in labor matters and was credited with the company's tough stand during a strike at two Dayton, Ohio, UAW-represented brake plants in March.
"Why would I want to talk to Harry Pearce? What has he got to do with it when I'm talking to his boss?" Yokich said.

The UAW chief said he has also not talked with J.T Battenberg, head of GM's Delphi Automotive Systems, which is comprised of GM's parts operations. Delphi is in the process of selling off several unprofitable operations that employ UAW members, and this has drawn the ire of UAW leaders.
"The only people I talk to is who I wish to talk to," Yokich said.
